2027-07-09.title: Friday of the seventh week after Pentecost
readings: God has shown mercy to all: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!”
Jesus is hungry and finds a fig tree with leaves but no fruit
2027-07-09.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Seventh Sunday after Pentecost. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam today.
2027-07-09.verse: For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be the glory forever. Amen.
theo: Today's Epistle is the end of a long argument. In chapters 9 to 11 of his Letter to the Romans, St Paul wrestles with a sorrow that lay close to his heart: most of his own people, the Jews, had not accepted Jesus as the Messiah, while many Gentiles had. Had God's promise failed? Paul will not allow it: “I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means! I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin.” And a few verses before today's passage he writes: “for the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.” The Church has taken these words very seriously. The Second Vatican Council, in Nostra Aetate 4, recalled that the Jewish people remain most dear to God, who does not repent of the gifts he makes or of the calls he issues (in substance), and that the Church can never forget that she received the revelation of the Old Testament through them. Against this background we hear today's verses: “Just as you were once disobedient to God but have now received mercy because of their disobedience, so they have now been disobedient in order that, by the mercy shown to you, they too may now receive mercy.” Paul sees history as one great movement of mercy in which no one has a claim and no one may boast, and he ends the thought with a sentence that holds the whole of the gospel: “For God has imprisoned all in disobedience so that he may be merciful to all.”

Then Paul, who has been reasoning for three chapters, simply stops reasoning and begins to sing: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” St John Chrysostom, commenting on this passage, remarked that when Paul's argument reaches the mystery of God's plan he does not try to measure it; he adores (Homilies on Romans, in substance). The questions he asks, “Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?” and “Or who has given a gift to him, to receive a gift in return?”, remind us that God owes us nothing and that every good thing is a gift. Then comes the line the Church loves to pray: “For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be the glory forever. Amen.” From him, because he is the source of all that exists; through him, because he sustains and redeems it; to him, because he is the end for which everything was made. In these weeks of the monsoon, when the rain pours on the hills and the paddy fields drink and turn green again, it is easy to feel this. No one gave the rain a gift first. All of it comes from him, and all of it is meant to rise again in thanksgiving. The great prayers of the Holy Qurbono end exactly as Paul does, with glory to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the people's Amen.

The Gospel is short and strange. “On the following day, when they came from Bethany, he was hungry. Seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see whether perhaps he would find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. He said to it, ‘May no one ever eat fruit from you again.’ And his disciples heard it.” St Mark places this story on either side of the cleansing of the Temple, and the two scenes are meant to be read together (Mark 11:15–17 and 11:20–24). The prophets often compared Israel to a fig tree from which God hoped for fruit (Hosea 9:10; Jeremiah 8:13), and Jesus here performs a prophetic sign, as the prophets did: an acted parable against religion that shows leaves and no fruit, splendid worship without justice, prayer and love. It is a warning for every believer, for each of us as much as for anyone, and it is no verdict on a people; Romans 11, which we heard first, forbids any Christian to think so. St Augustine, preaching on the fig tree, said that leaves without fruit are words without deeds (Sermon 89, in substance). Notice too that Jesus is hungry. He comes looking for us, hungry for our love, and the next morning the tree is found withered to its roots and he says to the disciples simply: “Have faith in God.” Let us ask ourselves today what fruit he would find in us, and let us give thanks that the God who is merciful to all keeps coming to us as one who hopes.
outline: Ask: if Jesus came to me hungry today, would he find fruit or only leaves?
God has imprisoned all in disobedience so that he may be merciful to all; no one has a claim and no one may boast.
Paul reasons, then adores: from him and through him and to him are all things.
The fig tree beside the Temple: prayer, justice and love are the fruit God looks for.
“For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be the glory forever. Amen.”
live: Before each meal this week add one sentence of praise: “From you and through you and to you are all things. Glory to you for ever. Amen.”
Choose one part of your life that has only leaves, a prayer said without attention, a promise not kept, a quarrel not mended, and begin to bear fruit in it.
Pray today for the Jewish people, from whom we received the Scriptures, and for anyone you have looked down on.
2027-07-09.prayer: Lord God, from you and through you and to you are all things. We bless you for the depth of your riches and wisdom and knowledge, and for the mercy you have shown to all. Keep us from boasting, since everything we have is your gift; keep us from leaves without fruit, and teach us to bear the fruit of prayer, justice and love. Remember your ancient people, whose gifts and calling you have never taken back, and gather all peoples in your mercy. To you be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono the great prayers rise into one long doxology, glory to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, now and always, and the people answer Amen with Paul; and from the altar the Lord gives us the fruit that never fails.

quick: St Paul says that God has shown mercy to all, and he breaks into praise: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!”
From him and through him and to him are all things: this is the Church's doxology, prayed at every Holy Qurbono.
Jesus, hungry, finds a fig tree with leaves but no fruit: God looks for fruit in us, not only for show.
2027-07-09.action: Say a short prayer of thanks today before you eat: from you and through you and to you are all things.
2027-07-09.question: If Jesus came to me hungry today, what would he find on my branches?

family.explain: St Paul looked at everything God has done and could only say: how deep is God's wisdom! Everything we have, our food, the rain, our home, our family, comes from God, goes through God's hands, and returns to God in thanks. In the Gospel, Jesus was hungry and went to a fig tree that had many leaves but no figs. Jesus wants more than leaves from us; he wants the fruits of kindness, prayer and sharing.
family.intention: We thank God for the rain and for our daily food, and we pray for those who have little.
family.ask: Ask: “What is one fruit of kindness we can bring to Jesus this week?”

illus: At a parish feast in a village near Thiruvalla the church was decorated with hundreds of paper flowers and strings of lights. Before the Qurbono the old sacristan stood at the door and looked at it all. Someone asked whether it was not beautiful. He said: it is beautiful, and the lights are for the eyes, but the Qurbono is for the hunger. He said the Lord came to the fig tree hungry, and what he looks for in a feast is not the lights but whether the people come hungry and go away fed, and whether the poor man at the gate has been fed too. Then he went in and lit the lamps on the altar one by one, saying that these at least were lit for the Lord.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, from you and through you and to you are all things. Make us glad in your mercy and fruitful in your service. Amen.
share: O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! (Romans 11:33). When have I been left without words before the mystery of God?
God has imprisoned all in disobedience so that he may be merciful to all (Romans 11:32). What does it mean to me that mercy is meant for everyone?
He found nothing but leaves (Mark 11:13). Where in my life are there leaves but no fruit?
pm.resp: Lord, make us fruitful in your service.
interc: For the Church, that she may offer to God the fruit of prayer, justice and love and not only outward show.
For the Jewish people, whose gifts and calling God has not withdrawn, and for the growth of respect and friendship between Jews and Christians.
For the hungry and the poor in the monsoon months, and for all who feed them.
For those who feel that God's ways are unsearchable in their own suffering, that they may be held in his mercy.
For our parish, that our feasts may feed the hungry and not only please the eye.
pm.close: Father, you shut up all in disobedience so that you might show mercy to all. Teach us to praise you for the depth of your wisdom and to bear the fruit you look for. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today St Paul comes to the end of a long argument, and he ends it with a song: O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! (Romans 11:33). He has been thinking about the people of Israel, about the Gentiles, and about the way God's plan moves through history. And at the end he does not say: now I understand it all. He says: now I can only praise.

He tells us what he has learned: God has imprisoned all in disobedience so that he may be merciful to all (Romans 11:32). Nobody can stand before God and say, I deserve this. We all live by mercy: those who came first and those who came later, Jew and Gentile, bishop and child. And the Church reminds us, with Paul, that the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (Romans 11:29). So no Christian may ever speak of the Jewish people with contempt or pride.

Then the Gospel gives us a picture to examine our own hearts. Jesus is hungry; he sees a fig tree in leaf and goes to it, but finds nothing but leaves (Mark 11:13). A tree that looks full of life and gives no fruit: that can be a person, a home, a parish. Fine words, fine feasts, fine decorations, and no prayer, no justice, no mercy. Jesus is not asking for more show. He is asking for fruit.

So let us ask ourselves where our leaves are, and with God's grace let us begin to bear fruit. And let us do what Paul does: let us thank God from whom, and through whom, and to whom are all things. To him be the glory for ever. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever gone to the mango tree hoping for a mango, and found only leaves? Jesus once did that with a fig tree! He was hungry, and the tree had lots of beautiful green leaves, but no figs. Jesus wants us to be like a tree full of fruit: not only looking nice, but being kind, sharing, praying and helping. And St Paul tells us to thank God for everything, because everything comes from him. This week, thank God for your food before you eat it, and do one kind thing that is like a fruit: share a sweet, help at home, or visit a lonely neighbour.

q: When I wanted to gather them, says the Lord, there are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree; even the leaves are withered, and what I gave them has passed away from them.
My Father is glorified by this, that you bear much fruit and become my disciples.

concl: God has imprisoned all in disobedience so that he may be merciful to all: we live by mercy, and mercy leaves no room for boasting.

2027-07-09.resolve: Praise God for his mercy, and bear fruit instead of leaves.
